questions.q: Which oxidation state of iron is required inside the protoporphyrin IX ring of hemoglobin and myoglobin to bind molecular oxygen reversibly?
options: Ferrous (Fe2+)
Ferric (Fe3+)
Elemental (Fe0)
Ferryl (Fe4+)
questions.explain: Only ferrous iron (Fe2+) in heme can form a reversible coordination bond with oxygen; oxidation to ferric iron (Fe3+) produces methemoglobin, which cannot bind oxygen.

open.q: State the oxidation state of iron required in hemoglobin to bind molecular oxygen reversibly.

questions.q: Which specific histidine residue in the globin pocket forms a direct covalent coordination bond with the fifth coordination site of heme iron?
options: Distal histidine (E7)
Proximal histidine (F8)
C-terminal histidine (HC3)
N-terminal valine
questions.explain: The proximal histidine (His F8) coordinates directly with the fifth coordination position of Fe2+, pulling the iron into the porphyrin plane upon oxygen binding to trigger allosteric subunit shifts.

open.q: Name the histidine residue in globin chains that coordinates directly with the fifth coordination site of heme iron.

questions.q: What is the primary structural role of the distal histidine (His E7) in myoglobin and hemoglobin?
options: Covalently anchors the vinyl side chains of protoporphyrin IX
Binds 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate in the central cavity
Forms a hydrogen bond with bound O2 and sterically hinders linear binding of carbon monoxide
Donates electrons to reduce ferric iron back to ferrous iron
questions.explain: The distal histidine (His E7) stabilizes bound bent O2 via hydrogen bonding while forcing carbon monoxide to bind at an angle, reducing CO affinity from ~25,000-fold in free heme to ~200-fold in intact hemoglobin.

open.q: Name the globin residue that forms a hydrogen bond with bound oxygen and sterically reduces carbon monoxide affinity.

questions.q: What is the polypeptide subunit composition of normal adult hemoglobin A (HbA)?
options: Two alpha and two gamma chains
Two alpha and two delta chains
Four beta chains
Two alpha and two beta chains
questions.explain: Adult hemoglobin A (HbA, ~97% of adult hemoglobin) is an alpha2-beta2 heterotetramer, whereas HbA2 is alpha2-delta2 (~2-3%) and fetal hemoglobin (HbF) is alpha2-gamma2.

open.q: State the globin chain composition of normal major adult hemoglobin (HbA).
accept: Two alpha and two beta chains

questions.q: Besides hemoglobin and myoglobin, which group of heme-containing enzymes utilizes heme iron cycling between Fe2+ and Fe3+ to transfer single electrons in the mitochondrial respiratory chain?
options: Cytochromes
Carbonic anhydrases
Superoxide dismutases
Glutathione peroxidases
questions.explain: Cytochromes (a, b, c) are haemoproteins whose iron reversibly alternates between ferrous (Fe2+) and ferric (Fe3+) states to carry electrons along the electron transport chain.

open.q: Name the class of electron-transferring haemoproteins in the electron transport chain whose iron cycles between Fe2+ and Fe3+.

questions.q: Why does hemoglobin exhibit a sigmoidal oxygen dissociation curve whereas myoglobin exhibits a hyperbolic curve?
options: Myoglobin has a higher P50 than hemoglobin
Hemoglobin is a tetramer exhibiting positive cooperativity as oxygen binding shifts it from the T (taut) state to the R (relaxed) state
Myoglobin binds four molecules of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate
Hemoglobin contains ferric iron while myoglobin contains ferrous iron
questions.explain: Binding of the first O2 molecule to deoxyhemoglobin (T state) pulls Fe2+ into the heme plane, breaking inter-subunit salt bridges and shifting the tetramer toward the high-affinity R state (Hill coefficient ~2.8).

open.q: What term describes the phenomenon in hemoglobin whereby binding of one oxygen molecule increases the oxygen affinity of the remaining subunits?

questions.q: How do elevated H+ (low pH) and increased PaCO2 facilitate oxygen unloading in metabolically active peripheral tissues (the Bohr effect)?
options: They covalently oxidize heme iron to Fe3+
They bind directly to the heme iron in place of oxygen
Protonation of specific histidine residues stabilizes salt bridges of the low-affinity T state, shifting the oxygen dissociation curve to the right
They stimulate red blood cell synthesis of fetal hemoglobin
questions.explain: In metabolically active tissues, high CO2 and H+ protonate residues such as His146 on beta-chains, stabilizing ionic salt bridges of the deoxy T state and shifting the curve rightward (increasing P50) to unload O2.

open.q: Name the physiological effect by which decreased pH and increased CO2 promote oxygen release from hemoglobin in peripheral tissues.

questions.q: Where does 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) bind on adult deoxyhemoglobin to decrease its oxygen affinity?
options: Directly to the sixth coordination site of each heme iron
To the exterior surface of the alpha chains
To the proximal histidine F8 residue
In the positively charged central cavity between the two beta-globin subunits
questions.explain: Negatively charged 2,3-BPG binds positively charged lysine and histidine residues lining the central cavity between the beta chains of T-state deoxyhemoglobin, stabilizing the T state and promoting O2 unloading.

open.q: Between which two globin subunits does 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate bind in the central cavity of adult deoxyhemoglobin?

questions.q: Why does fetal hemoglobin (HbF, alpha2-gamma2) have a higher oxygen affinity than maternal adult hemoglobin (HbA, alpha2-beta2)?
options: Gamma-globin chains have serine instead of histidine at position 143, reducing positive charge and lowering affinity for 2,3-BPG
HbF lacks proximal histidine residues
HbF binds eight molecules of oxygen per tetramer
Fetal erythrocytes lack carbonic anhydrase
questions.explain: Replacing positively charged His143 in beta chains with neutral Ser143 in gamma chains weakens 2,3-BPG binding to HbF, keeping HbF shifted toward the high-affinity R state to extract O2 across the placenta.

open.q: Which amino acid substitution in gamma-globin chains (replacing His143 of beta-globin) decreases 2,3-BPG binding to fetal hemoglobin?

questions.q: How is the majority of carbon dioxide transported in venous blood from peripheral tissues to the lungs?
options: Dissolved physically in plasma
As plasma bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) generated via erythrocyte carbonic anhydrase and exported via the chloride shift
Bound directly to heme iron as carboxyhemoglobin
Bound to plasma albumin
questions.explain: About 70-80% of CO2 enters RBCs, is hydrated by carbonic anhydrase to H2CO3, dissociates into H+ (buffered by deoxyhemoglobin) and HCO3-, and exits into plasma in exchange for Cl- via Band 3 (AE1); ~10-15% forms carbaminohemoglobin on N-terminal amino groups.

open.q: In what chemical form is approximately 70 to 80% of carbon dioxide transported in blood from tissues to the lungs?

questions.q: In which two subcellular compartments do the eight enzymatic steps of heme biosynthesis occur?
options: Nucleus and Golgi apparatus
Rough endoplasmic reticulum and lysosomes
Mitochondria and cytosol
Peroxisomes and plasma membrane
questions.explain: The first step (ALA synthase) and final three steps (coproporphyrinogen oxidase, protoporphyrinogen oxidase, ferrochelatase) occur in mitochondria, while the four intermediate steps occur in the cytosol.

open.q: Name the two cellular compartments across which the pathway of heme biosynthesis is divided.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of heme synthesis by condensing glycine and succinyl-CoA into delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA)?
options: ALA dehydratase
Porphobilinogen deaminase
Ferrochelatase
ALA synthase
questions.explain: Delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS1 in liver, ALAS2 in erythroid precursors) requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) and catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting step of heme synthesis.

open.q: Name the rate-limiting enzyme of heme biosynthesis.

questions.q: How is hepatic ALA synthase (ALAS1) regulated differently from erythroid ALA synthase (ALAS2)?
options: ALAS1 is feedback-inhibited and transcriptionally repressed by heme (hematin) and induced by CYP450-inducing drugs, whereas ALAS2 is regulated by intracellular iron availability via iron-responsive elements
ALAS1 is activated by heme, whereas ALAS2 is inhibited by heme
ALAS1 is located in the cytosol, whereas ALAS2 is in the nucleus
ALAS1 requires biotin, whereas ALAS2 requires vitamin B12
questions.explain: In hepatocytes, free heme represses ALAS1 transcription, blocks its mitochondrial import, and inhibits its activity; in developing erythroblasts, iron deficiency stabilizes IRP binding to the 5'-IRE of ALAS2 mRNA to prevent excess protoporphyrin synthesis without iron.

open.q: What clinical therapeutic agent (oxidized heme) is infused in acute intermittent porphyria to repress hepatic ALAS1?

questions.q: Which mitochondrial enzyme catalyzes the final step of heme biosynthesis by inserting ferrous iron (Fe2+) into protoporphyrin IX?
options: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase
Ferrochelatase
ALA dehydratase
Protoporphyrinogen oxidase
questions.explain: Ferrochelatase (heme synthase) inserts Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX; its inhibition by lead or genetic deficiency in erythropoietic protoporphyria causes accumulation of free erythrocyte protoporphyrin.

open.q: Name the final enzyme of heme biosynthesis that inserts ferrous iron into protoporphyrin IX.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child living in an old building with peeling paint presents with microcytic anemia, basophilic stippling of erythrocytes, abdominal colic, and elevated blood free erythrocyte protoporphyrin and urinary delta-ALA. Which two heme synthesis enzymes are inhibited?
options: ALA synthase and PBG deaminase
Uroporphyrinogen III synthase and coproporphyrinogen oxidase
ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase
Heme oxygenase and biliverdin reductase
questions.explain: Lead binds sulfhydryl groups and displaces zinc in cytoplasmic ALA dehydratase (elevating delta-ALA) and inhibits mitochondrial ferrochelatase (elevating protoporphyrin IX and causing sideroblastic anemia).

open.q: Name the two enzymes in heme biosynthesis inhibited by lead poisoning.

questions.q: A 27-year-old woman develops severe abdominal pain, constipation, peripheral neuropathy, and acute psychosis after taking phenobarbital. Her urine turns dark reddish-brown upon standing, and she has no skin photosensitivity. Which enzyme is deficient?
options: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase
Ferrochelatase
ALA dehydratase
Porphobilinogen deaminase
questions.explain: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is an autosomal dominant deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase (hydroxymethylbilane synthase), causing accumulation of early non-photoreactive neurotoxic precursors (ALA and PBG).

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme causes acute intermittent porphyria?

questions.q: Why do late-step porphyrias such as porphyria cutanea tarda (uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency) cause blistering cutaneous photosensitivity, whereas acute intermittent porphyria does not?
options: Cyclic tetrapyrrole porphyrinogens oxidize to conjugated porphyrins that absorb ~400 nm light and generate reactive oxygen species in the skin, whereas linear precursors ALA and PBG do not absorb light
Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase is expressed only in epidermal keratinocytes
ALA and PBG are excreted exclusively in sweat
Porphyria cutanea tarda causes severe iron deficiency
questions.explain: Early precursors (ALA and PBG) are non-cyclic and non-fluorescent, causing neurovisceral symptoms only; downstream tetrapyrrole rings (uroporphyrin, coproporphyrin, protoporphyrin) absorb Soret-band light (~400 nm) and generate tissue-damaging singlet oxygen.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme causes porphyria cutanea tarda?

questions.q: What is the exact molecular mutation responsible for sickle cell hemoglobin (HbS)?
options: Substitution of lysine for glutamate at position 6 of the beta-globin chain
Substitution of valine for glutamate at position 6 of the beta-globin chain
Deletion of both alpha-globin genes on chromosome 16
Substitution of tyrosine for proximal histidine F8
questions.explain: In HbS (Glu6Val in beta-globin), replacing hydrophilic negatively charged glutamate with hydrophobic valine creates a sticky hydrophobic patch on deoxygenated HbS that polymerizes into rigid fibers.

open.q: State the specific amino acid substitution in the beta-globin chain that produces hemoglobin S (HbS).

questions.q: How does hydroxyurea reduce vaso-occlusive crises in patients with sickle cell disease?
options: Directly chelates ferrous iron in HbS
Converts valine-6 back to glutamate via post-translational modification
Increases synthesis of fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which interferes with deoxy-HbS polymerization
Inhibits red cell 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate synthesis
questions.explain: Hydroxyurea induces gamma-globin expression and raises HbF levels; alpha2-gamma2 and hybrid alpha2-betaS-gamma tetramers cannot incorporate into deoxy-HbS polymers, preventing red cell sickling.

open.q: Which type of hemoglobin is upregulated by hydroxyurea therapy to inhibit HbS polymerization in sickle cell disease?

questions.q: In hemoglobin C disease (HbC), which amino acid replaces glutamate at position 6 of the beta-globin chain, leading to intracellular rod-shaped HbC crystals and target cells?
options: Valine
Alanine
Aspartate
Lysine
questions.explain: HbC results from a Glu6Lys substitution in beta-globin, reducing solubility and causing electrostatic crystallization of HbC within erythrocytes and mild chronic hemolytic anemia.

open.q: Which amino acid replaces glutamate at position 6 of the beta-globin chain in hemoglobin C?

questions.q: Why does beta-thalassemia major typically become clinically apparent at 4 to 6 months of age rather than at birth?
options: High fetal hemoglobin (HbF, alpha2-gamma2) levels at birth compensate for absent beta-globin until gamma-globin synthesis declines after infancy
Maternal IgG protects fetal red cells until 6 months
Beta-globin genes are not inherited until after birth
Bone marrow erythropoiesis does not begin until 6 months
questions.explain: Fetal hemoglobin uses gamma-globin rather than beta-globin; symptoms appear around 6 months when physiological hemoglobin switching from gamma to beta fails, leaving unpaired alpha-globin chains to precipitate.

open.q: Which insoluble globin chains precipitate inside erythroid precursors to cause ineffective erythropoiesis in beta-thalassemia major?

questions.q: In four-gene deletion alpha-thalassemia (hydrops fetalis), which abnormal homotetramer forms in utero and causes severe fetal hypoxia due to its extremely high oxygen affinity?
options: Hemoglobin H (beta4)
Hemoglobin Bart (gamma4)
Hemoglobin A2 (alpha2-delta2)
Hemoglobin S (alpha2-betaS2)
questions.explain: Complete absence of alpha-globin chains in utero forces excess fetal gamma chains to form gamma4 tetramers (Hb Bart), which lack cooperativity and hold oxygen so tightly that tissues suffer fatal hypoxia.

open.q: Name the abnormal gamma-globin homotetramer (gamma4) formed in severe four-gene deletion alpha-thalassemia.

questions.q: What characteristic hemoglobin electrophoresis finding supports the diagnosis of beta-thalassemia minor (trait)?
options: Markedly elevated HbS (>80%)
Presence of Hb Bart
Elevated HbA2 (>3.5%) and mildly elevated HbF
Complete absence of HbA
questions.explain: Reduced synthesis of one beta-globin allele allows excess alpha chains to pair with delta and gamma chains, raising HbA2 (alpha2-delta2) above 3.5%.

open.q: Which minor adult hemoglobin fraction (alpha2-delta2) is classically elevated over 3.5% on electrophoresis in beta-thalassemia trait?

questions.q: A 22-year-old patient treated with dapsone develops central cyanosis unresponsive to 100% supplemental oxygen, chocolate-brown arterial blood, and an oxygen saturation gap on pulse oximetry. Which enzyme system normally prevents this condition, and what is the first-line antidote?
options: Superoxide dismutase; N-acetylcysteine
Carbonic anhydrase; sodium bicarbonate
Ferrochelatase; deferoxamine
Cytochrome b5 reductase (NADH-methemoglobin reductase); methylene blue
questions.explain: Oxidizing drugs like dapsone, benzocaine, and nitrates oxidize heme Fe2+ to Fe3+ (methemoglobinemia); NADH-dependent cytochrome b5 reductase normally reduces Fe3+ back to Fe2+, and intravenous methylene blue accelerates NADPH-methemoglobin reductase to restore Fe2+.

open.q: Name the first-line intravenous antidote used to treat acquired methemoglobinemia.

questions.q: How does carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning impair tissue oxygen delivery in two distinct ways?
options: Competes with O2 at heme binding sites with ~200-fold higher affinity AND locks remaining subunits in the high-affinity R state, shifting the oxygen dissociation curve to the left
Oxidizes all heme iron to Fe3+ and precipitates globin chains
Cleaves protoporphyrin IX and depletes 2,3-BPG
Inhibits carbonic anhydrase and causes severe metabolic alkalosis
questions.explain: CO binds heme Fe2+ ~200 times more tightly than O2 and allosterically stabilizes the R state of partially occupied hemoglobin tetramers, preventing the remaining bound O2 from unloading in peripheral tissues.

open.q: In which direction (left or right) does carbon monoxide shift the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve of the remaining oxygen-binding sites?

questions.q: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) is formed non-enzymatically by the attachment of glucose to which specific amino acid residue of the beta-globin chain?
options: Proximal histidine (F8)
N-terminal valine
Glutamate-6
Cysteine-93
questions.explain: Glucose forms a reversible Schiff base with the N-terminal valine of beta-globin that undergoes an Amadori rearrangement into a stable ketoamine (HbA1c), reflecting average glycemia over the ~120-day erythrocyte lifespan.

open.q: Name the N-terminal amino acid residue of the beta-globin chain that undergoes non-enzymatic glycation to form HbA1c.

questions.q: Which microsomal enzyme in reticuloendothelial macrophages catalyzes the rate-limiting step of heme degradation, cleaving the porphyrin ring into biliverdin, ferrous iron, and carbon monoxide?
options: Biliverdin reductase
UDP-glucuronosyltransferase
Heme oxygenase
Ferrochelatase
questions.explain: Heme oxygenase uses NADPH and O2 to oxidize the alpha-methene bridge of heme, releasing green biliverdin, Fe2+ (recycled via transferrin/ferritin), and carbon monoxide.

open.q: Name the enzyme in macrophages that cleaves the heme ring to produce biliverdin, iron, and carbon monoxide.

questions.q: Which cytosolic NADPH-dependent enzyme reduces green biliverdin into orange-yellow unconjugated bilirubin in macrophages?
options: Heme oxygenase
Beta-glucuronidase
Cytochrome P450 reductase
Biliverdin reductase
questions.explain: Biliverdin reductase reduces the central methene bridge of biliverdin using NADPH to yield lipophilic unconjugated bilirubin.

open.q: Name the NADPH-dependent enzyme that reduces biliverdin to unconjugated bilirubin.

questions.q: Why is unconjugated bilirubin neurotoxic to neonates (kernicterus) when its plasma concentration exceeds albumin-binding capacity?
options: It is lipophilic, crosses the immature blood-brain barrier, and deposits in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei where it uncouples oxidative phosphorylation
It is water-soluble and clogs cerebral ventricles
It directly activates NMDA receptors in the cortex
It destroys myelin via autoimmune antibodies
questions.explain: Free unbound unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and penetrates the neonatal blood-brain barrier, injuring mitochondria and neurons in the basal ganglia (globus pallidus) and subthalamic nuclei.

open.q: Name the neurological syndrome caused by deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the neonatal basal ganglia and brainstem.

questions.q: How does blue-light phototherapy (wavelength ~450-460 nm) reduce serum unconjugated bilirubin in neonatal jaundice?
options: Induces hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase transcription
Photoisomerizes insoluble Z,Z-bilirubin in skin capillaries into water-soluble structural and configurational isomers (such as lumirubin) that can be excreted in bile and urine without conjugation
Oxidizes bilirubin directly into carbon dioxide
Increases serum albumin synthesis
questions.explain: Blue light converts native 4Z,15Z-bilirubin into polar photoisomers (4Z,15E-bilirubin and irreversible cyclized lumirubin) that bypass hepatic glucuronidation for biliary and renal excretion.

open.q: Name the irreversible water-soluble structural photoisomer of bilirubin formed during neonatal phototherapy.

questions.q: What is the fate of conjugated bilirubin after it is secreted into the duodenum via bile?
options: It is reabsorbed intact in the stomach
It is converted back into heme by pancreatic lipase

Intestinal bacteria deconjugate and reduce it to colorless urobilinogens, most of which oxidize to brown stercobilin in stool while a fraction undergoes enterohepatic recirculation or renal excretion as urobilin
It is degraded into urea by enterocytes
questions.explain: Colonic anaerobes remove glucuronide groups and reduce bilirubin to urobilinogen; ~80% is excreted as brown stercobilin in feces, ~15-20% enters enterohepatic circulation, and ~2-5% is filtered by kidneys as yellow urobilin.

open.q: Name the brown pigment formed by intestinal bacterial metabolism of bilirubin that gives normal feces its color.

questions.q: A 15-year-old girl presents with asymptomatic fluctuating jaundice since childhood. Laboratory workup shows total bilirubin of 4.2 mg/dL with 3.6 mg/dL conjugated (direct), normal liver transaminases, and a grossly black-pigmented liver on biopsy due to impaired canalicular excretion. Which syndrome does she have?
options: Gilbert syndrome
Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I
Rotor syndrome
Dubin-Johnson syndrome
questions.explain: Dubin-Johnson syndrome is an autosomal recessive mutation in the canalicular multidrug resistance-associated protein 2 (MRP2 / ABCC2) transporter, causing conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and black melanin-like pigment deposition in lysosomes (unlike Rotor syndrome, which lacks black liver pigmentation).

open.q: Name the hereditary conjugated hyperbilirubinemia caused by MRP2 transporter deficiency that produces a characteristic black liver.

questions.q: How do Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I and Crigler-Najjar syndrome type II differ in severity and response to phenobarbital?
options: Type I has complete absence of UGT1A1 with fatal kernicterus risk and no response to phenobarbital, whereas Type II has partial UGT1A1 activity that improves with phenobarbital induction
Type I causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, whereas Type II causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia
Type I is X-linked, whereas Type II is mitochondrial
Type I responds completely to phenobarbital, whereas Type II requires liver transplantation
questions.explain: Crigler-Najjar type I lacks any functional UGT1A1 gene product so enzyme inducers like phenobarbital cannot increase conjugation, whereas type II retains ~10% residual UGT1A1 activity that can be induced by phenobarbital.

open.q: Which barbiturate enzyme inducer reduces serum bilirubin in Crigler-Najjar syndrome type II and Gilbert syndrome by upregulating UGT1A1?

questions.q: Which four substituent side chains are attached to the eight beta-carbons of the four pyrrole rings in protoporphyrin IX?
options: Four methyl, two vinyl, and two propionate groups
Four ethyl, two acetyl, and two methyl groups
Four propionate, two vinyl, and two hydroxyl groups
Eight methyl groups
questions.explain: Protoporphyrin IX contains four methyl (-CH3), two vinyl (-CH=CH2), and two propionate (-CH2CH2COO-) side chains arranged asymmetrically (type IX isomer) around the tetrapyrrole macrocycle.

open.q: List the three types of substituent side chains attached to the pyrrole rings of protoporphyrin IX.

questions.q: What is the Haldane effect in pulmonary capillaries?
options: High CO2 increases hemoglobin affinity for oxygen
Oxygenation of hemoglobin in the lungs promotes dissociation of H+ and CO2 (carbaminohemoglobin) from hemoglobin to facilitate CO2 exhalation
2,3-BPG increases oxygen binding in the lungs
Low temperature decreases hemoglobin oxygen affinity
questions.explain: The Haldane effect is the reciprocal of the Bohr effect: binding of O2 shifts hemoglobin to the R state, breaking salt bridges to release Bohr protons (which combine with HCO3- to form CO2) and decreasing carbamino-CO2 binding.

open.q: Name the physiological effect whereby oxygenation of hemoglobin in the lungs promotes the release of carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions.

questions.q: Why does acute alcohol ingestion or fasting frequently precipitate acute neurovisceral attacks in patients with acute intermittent porphyria?
options: Alcohol directly destroys bone marrow erythroblasts
Fasting and alcohol induce PGC-1alpha and hepatic ALAS1 transcription, increasing flux through the blocked pathway and accumulating neurotoxic ALA and PBG
Alcohol inhibits renal excretion of conjugated bilirubin
Fasting increases insulin levels which activate ALA synthase
questions.explain: Fasting induces hepatic PGC-1alpha, which coactivates transcription of ALAS1; carbohydrate loading (intravenous glucose) suppresses PGC-1alpha and downregulates ALAS1 during acute attacks.

open.q: Which intravenous nutritional therapy is administered alongside hemin during an acute porphyria attack to suppress PGC-1alpha-mediated induction of hepatic ALAS1?

questions.q: What physiological and environmental factors trigger polymerization of deoxy-HbS and vaso-occlusive sickling crises in patients with sickle cell disease?
options: Alkalosis, hyperoxia, and overhydration
High fetal hemoglobin and low 2,3-BPG
Hypothermia and low intracellular HbS concentration
Hypoxia, acidosis, dehydration (increased intracellular HbS concentration), and fever/infection
questions.explain: Deoxygenation, acidosis (Bohr shift to T state), cellular dehydration (raising intracellular HbS concentration), and infection promote the deoxy T conformation of HbS required for polymer nucleation.

open.q: Which conformational state of hemoglobin S (T or R) undergoes polymerization to cause erythrocyte sickling?

questions.q: Why should methylene blue be avoided in a patient with methemoglobinemia who also has severe glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency?
options: Methylene blue requires NADPH (generated by G6PD) to be reduced to leukomethylene blue, so it is ineffective and can worsen oxidative hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
Methylene blue irreversibly binds hemoglobin A2
G6PD-deficient patients lack cytochrome b5 reductase completely
Methylene blue converts methemoglobin into carboxyhemoglobin
questions.explain: Methylene blue acts as an electron shuttle using NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway; in severe G6PD deficiency, NADPH is lacking and methylene blue acts as an oxidant causing hemolysis (ascorbic acid is used instead).

open.q: Which vitamin antioxidant can be used as an alternative treatment for methemoglobinemia in patients with severe G6PD deficiency?

questions.q: Which laboratory profile of serum bilirubin and urine findings characterizes pre-hepatic (hemolytic) jaundice?
options: Markedly elevated conjugated bilirubin, positive urine bilirubin, and absent urine urobilinogen
Predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, negative urine bilirubin, and elevated urine urobilinogen
Equal elevation of conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin with acholic stools
Normal serum bilirubin with massive bilirubinuria
questions.explain: In hemolytic jaundice, excess unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound (hence absent from urine), while increased hepatic conjugation and biliary excretion generate excess intestinal urobilinogen that is reabsorbed and excreted in urine.

open.q: Is urinary bilirubin positive or negative in pure pre-hepatic (hemolytic) jaundice?

questions.q: Which peroxisomal haemoprotein rapidly decomposes toxic hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) into water and molecular oxygen?
options: Myeloperoxidase
Cytochrome c oxidase
Catalase
Nitric oxide synthase
questions.explain: Catalase is a tetrameric heme-containing enzyme abundant in peroxisomes and erythrocytes that catalyzes 2 H2O2 -> 2 H2O + O2 at one of the highest turnover rates of any known enzyme.

open.q: Name the peroxisomal haemoprotein enzyme that converts hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
